LA CROSSE, Wis. (WXOW) - The state of Wisconsin can take legal action if a student threatens school safety, but first they look at the student's age, family situation, behavioral history and severity of the threat.
La Crosse County District Attorney Tim Gruenke said there have been a number of school threats throughout his time in the area, but few warranted legal action.
"It's more of a try to scare people, a try to get attention, trying to get back at someone and things like that," Gruenke said. "We still have to address it and take it serious but we've had very few that have gotten to a point to actually use a weapon."
When credible threats come through, Wisconsin students 17 and older would be charged as an adult.
Students ages 16 and below could face adult criminal charges if their threats are deemed as 'attempted homicide'. However, anything less severe would vary depending on the situation.
"If it gets below that [homicide or attempted homicide] it's a little bit harder to charge them as an adult and you might need the court's permission to do so," Gruenke said. "It involves the child's psychological makeup, the seriousness of the charge, any history that they have and factors like that."
He said minors under 16 would most likely see 'disorderly conduct' charges for harassments, bomb scares, or terrorist threats brought against them.
"These days especially with recent events in Michigan, you can be rest assured schools and police are going to be reacting very quickly, being very cautious and applying whatever laws we can make sure that we can keep people safe," he said.
The West Salem School District caught a red flag situation early in September.
"Thankfully we have a very good relationship with our school resource officer and the West Salem Police Department," Superintendent Ryan Rieber said. "So we're able to have quick conversations with them if something were to come through or if they would get wind of something or vice versa."
Gruenke said it is usually up to the school whether or not they think criminal charges are necessary, but most of the time it's about attention.
"We try to get students the help that they need," he said. "It's usually actually a cry for help or a fit of anger that's resulting from some other disfunction in their lives. We've had very few true threats where someone actually had access to a weapon and intended to use it."
He said West Salem, Onalaska and other La Crosse County school districts are well prepared and handled previous threats adequately.
He said it is still important that parents, teachers and the community pay attention to any student behavior changes.

Rutherford County Schools closely monitoring threats of potential social media challenge
State law enforcement officials are reporting that social media influencers may have issued a challenge encouraging students to make fake social media threats toward schools for Friday.
Rutherford County Schools sent an email to parents Wednesday alerting them to the situation. The district is working closely with the Rutherford County Sheriff's Office to monitor the situation and no credible threats have been issued, a district official assured.
“With all communications of this type, Rutherford County Sheriff’s Office takes these seriously and our school resource officers, patrol and detective divisions are monitoring the information very closely,” Sheriff Mike Fitzhugh said.
Intent of the challenge is to create worry and panic to disrupt school Friday, a district official explained in the email.
In the email, parents are asked to discuss appropriate social media behavior with their children and to encourage them not to participate in the spreading of false information or social media pranks in an attempt to disrupt school.
Any social media threats made against schools will be fully investigated. Any students found responsible for making threats or spreading false rumors as a prank will be disciplined accordingly and will likely face criminal charges as well.
“School safety is our top priority, and these types of pranks aren’t funny and will not be tolerated,” Director of Schools Bill Spurlock said. “We know parents also value safe learning environments for their children, and we appreciate their assistance with this matter.”
On Monday, two Rutherford County middle school students were arrested for making social media threats over the weekend.
One of the students attends Blackman Middle and the other Whitworth-Buchanan Middle. Both will be taken to Juvenile Court, according to a press release from Lisa Marchesoni, a spokesperson with the Rutherford County Sheriff's Office.
School Resource Officer Joey Vann arrested the Blackman Middle student on charges of sending out “Snap Chats” specifically directed to a group of fellow students, according to the press release.
The social media threats did not involve injuries.
Deputies, however, have dealt with campus violence, including Sept. 14 after the stabbing of a Rocky Fork Middle student, who was treated and released from TriStar StoneCrest Medical Center in Smyrna. The sheriff's office charged another student with attempted first-degree murder in that case.

Pittsburgh area school districts monitoring TikTok post that threatens school safety
Several districts in the area have sent letters to families telling them they are aware of a post that has been shared widely this week on the social media platform TikTok.
School districts in the Pittsburgh area are monitoring a TikTok post that threatens school safety on Friday.
Several districts in the western Pennsylvania region have sent letters to families telling them they are aware of a post that has been shared widely this week on the social media platform TikTok.
The districts said the post refers to a threat to school safety "for every school in the USA, even elementary," on Friday, Dec. 17.
TikTok posted a statement on Twitter, saying in part that it was working with law enforcement to investigate. "We handle even rumored threats with utmost seriousness, which is why we're working with law enforcement to look into warnings about potential violence at schools even though we have not found evidence of such threats originating or spreading via TikTok," the tweet said.
Pittsburgh's Action News 4 talked with Norwin parents as they learned about the threats.
"I don't know what the answer is. I have two boys. They both have gone to Norwin. I have many conversations with them about how to handle themselves, what to do in case of an emergency, but yeah, it's very concerning," Allen Carney said.
"There can be situations where somebody might post something on social media and you think it's a joke and it ends up being a disaster," Kim Francis said.
The threats are not specific to one school.
The districts said the post appears to be part of a national TikTok trend and did not originate from school districts in the Pittsburgh area.
"While we do not believe the threat to be credible, we are closely monitoring the situation and taking it seriously. Additionally, District Safety and Security staff are aware of these threats and will be monitoring for any suspicious activity. We request that only scheduled visitors come to District facilities tomorrow," a letter from the Upper St. Clair School District said in part.
Meanwhile, the Charleroi School District will be moving to virtual learning on Friday out of an abundance of caution. The district said it was notified by the Pennsylvania Department of Education and Pennsylvania State Police about the numerous messages that are circulating on social media regarding threats to schools on Friday.
The Gateway School District also announced that Gateway High School will be moving to remote/virtual instruction on Friday following the social media threat identified on Dec. 17.
Pittsburgh Public Schools said its school police have been in contact with City Police regarding the post and will be on heightened alert.
The Mount Lebanon School District also posted a message to families online saying in part that while they do not believe the threat to be credible, they are closely monitoring the situation and taking it seriously.
The district said it has contacted the Mount Lebanon police department regarding the post and they may have an increased police presence in and around school buildings on Friday as an added precaution.
The Bethel Park School District also told parents in an email that they will have an increased police presence in buildings on Friday out of an abundance of caution.
The Norwin School District also sent an email to families, saying it is collaborating with the North Huntingdon Township Police Department regarding the issue.
Parents at the district said it was assuring that schools across the region were taking each threat seriously.
"I think every situation is going to need to be evaluated. You can't cancel school every time somebody post about a threat, otherwise, you are not going to have school," Carney said.
"I feel like it depends on the situation, but everyone should be vigilant and keep their eyes open," Francis said.
Many of the districts told families that this incident serves as a good example of why it is important to avoid sharing posts online that refer to school safety threats.
"Even if they are not credible, these posts can cause a great deal of stress and anxiety for our students, families and staff. We ask our families to monitor their children's social media activity and speak with them about what is and is not appropriate when interacting online," one district said in a letter to families.
As of Friday morning, Leechburg and Kiski Area School Districts said they will have additional security.
North Hills, Plum, and Highlands school districts also said they will have an increased security presence.
Seneca Valley School District said it is moving to a fully remote instructional model Friday for all students K-12. Students will begin the virtual day on a two hour delay.
Keystone Oaks reached out to Pittsburgh's Action News 4 saying students would be participating in online learning Friday.
Pittsburgh Public Schools will be operating on a modified lockdown Friday in response to the threat. This means students will remain inside buildings all day and only visitors with a prior appointment are permitted to enter the building.
Brian Kohlhepp with the Ross Township police department said although there were no threats directly affecting the North Hills School District, they are not taking any chances. The department increased patrols in the area and the north hills school district has its own police department.
He said, “We have to treat these seriously, obviously the security of our schools and making sure that our kids are safe is something that the Ross Police and the North Hills School district take seriously."

'Safety is a priority': How Lansing area schools, police prepare for active shooter threats
If there were to be a threat inside Ovid-Elsie schools, Superintendent Ryan Cunningham feels confident students and teachers would know what to do to stay safe.
They do drills multiple times a year — both in the middle of class and during lunch or passing time — and have installed the SmartBoot system, created by a Fowlerville company, throughout the district.
If anyone deploys the "boot" — a small steel plate that can barricade a door and make it nearly impossible to open — in a classroom, it sets off an alarm throughout the school with flashing red lights and a verbal "lockdown" alert, Cunningham said.

About the victims: Oxford shooting deaths include honor student, athletes and artist
4 dead, 7 injured: Oxford High School shooting is nation's deadliest school shooting since 2018
Teachers can use a tablet to request help or call 911 and Cunningham can view where the call for help originated, he said. If the "boot" is deployed, all administrators within the district will know.
"It's a pretty slick system," Cunningham said.
Ovid-Elsie bought this system, as well as strong blast shields for doors and windows, with the help of a state grant, Cunningham said. Their cameras, which have been upgraded so they have no blind spots, are linked to dispatch so law enforcement can access the feed if needed.
Ovid-Elsie schools work with local police departments, the Clinton County Sheriff's Department and county dispatch to make sure everyone knows the plan should there be any kind of attack on a school, like there was in Oxford on Tuesday afternoon.
Four teenagers — Hana St. Juliana, 14, Tate Myre, 16, Madisyn Baldwin, 17, and Justin Shilling, 17 — were at Oxford High School. A 15-year-old student has been charged with terrorism, four counts of murder, seven counts of attempted murder and 12 felony weapons charges.
Training in schools
The way Ovid-Elsie has trained to handle school shootings is similar to many other districts, though most do not have the same technology.
Schools are required to conduct at least three school safety and security drills yearly, state Superintendent Michael Rice wrote in an email to districts.
In Charlotte, teachers and staff annually review emergency action plans, Superintendent Mandy Stewart said. Teachers have applications on their phones where they can send the school into lockdown, if needed. The app allows teachers to communicate with both the district and local law enforcement so they know when it is safe to come out.
"We think it's important that a lockdown can get called from any staff member, not just the main office," Stewart said.
She attended a lockdown drill Monday at the high school. As she walked through the hallways checking doors, it was quiet. Students acted as they should, she said.
"I do think the students are prepared, but that's why we need to do reviews and training," Stewart said. "I think it's important for the community to know that we are aware of concerns that happen and we are vigilant in making sure students and staff alike know how to respond in a crisis ... Our safety is a priority. We are doing everything in our power to make sure students and staff are safe."
Local police departments or sheriff's offices said they work closely with schools to ensure they have a plan in place for active violence.
Ingham County Sheriff's Department Capt. Andy Daenzer said while they offer advice to districts on how to best respond to active violence, it is up to administrators to determine the district's action plan.
Meridian Township Sgt. Ed Besonen said each year he sits down with someone from each school district to talk about emergency plans and drills for the upcoming school year. When they run drills, officers are present to make sure things are being done properly.
Lansing Police Public Information Director Robert Merritt said they train yearly with other law enforcement agencies in the area on how to handle active violence at places like schools, businesses, theaters and concerts.
They use empty school buildings and offices during the scenario-based training to make it as realistic as possible, Merritt said.
Eaton County first responders have done trainings at Charlotte High School with actor patients, fake bombs and hostage situations, Eaton County Sheriff Tom Reich said.
It's all preparedness, not prevention, he said.
"You never know when things are going to happen," Reich said.
'We really can't train ourselves out of this tragedy'
Even in Oxford, where first responders handled the situation "perfectly," it still wasn't enough to keep every student safe, Oakland County Prosecutor Karen McDonald said during a press conference Wednesday.
"The response was executed perfectly, yet three, four children were killed and multiple injuries occurred, which suggests that we really can't train ourselves out of this tragedy," McDonald said.
Students and teachers used what they had been taught during trainings and turned their desks to the side and barricaded the door, Oakland County Sheriff Michael Bouchard said during a press conference. That saved lives. Police saw gunshots had been fired through doors and barricades.
"The best preventive path we've seen that has worked is to make sure everyone talks about something they've seen, heard or witnessed so it can get looked into, to put training and protocols in place," Bouchard said Wednesday.
But more needs to be done than just training in schools, Michigan State University psychology professors John Carlson and Sydney Nelson and Towson University professor HaeDong Kim found.
Their studies suggested school safety is maximized when the school's physical environment, procedures and mental health treatment is "hardened," they wrote. Hardening the school's physical environment involves things like increased technology, metal detectors, locked doors and security cameras.
Cathy Brunton's granddaughter goes to Holt High School. She said she worries for the girl's safety.
Last month her granddaughter saw on social media that there would be some sort of gang fight that day, Brunton said. Scared, she didn't attend school.
Brunton said she wants to see metal detectors installed at schools to ensure the safety of students.
